deities.about: Lord of beginnings and remover of obstacles, so every puja begins with him. Son of Shiv and Parvati, he rides a mouse and loves modak.
The preserver, who takes avatars such as Ram and Krishna whenever dharma is in danger. He rests on the serpent Shesh, with Lakshmi at his feet.
The great ascetic of Kailash, destroyer of ignorance and the kindest of gods to his devotees. The Ganga flows from his hair and the crescent moon rests on his brow.
The Mother Goddess who rides a lion and defeated Mahishasur. Navratri, her nine nights, is one of the great festivals of the year.
Goddess of wealth, fortune and grace, consort of Vishnu. She is welcomed into every home with lamps on Diwali night.
Goddess of learning, speech and music, who holds the veena and rides a swan. Students pray to her before study, especially on Basant Panchami.
Son of the wind god, devoted servant of Shri Ram, and a symbol of strength and fearlessness. He carried the mountain of herbs to save Lakshman.

img.cap: Hanuman fetches the herb-bearing mountain, Ravi Varma Press, 1910s

deities.about: The seventh avatar of Vishnu and the ideal king of the Ramayan, worshipped with Sita, Lakshman and Hanuman as the Ram Panchayatan.
The eighth avatar of Vishnu: the butter-stealing child of Gokul, the flute player of Vrindavan, and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gita.
The Sun, the visible god, worshipped at sunrise with water offerings. The Gayatri mantra is addressed to him as Savitr, and Chhath is his great festival.

img.cap: Surya in his chariot, late 19th century

deities.label: Universal prayers
deities.about: Prayers addressed to God in any form, sung by people of every tradition.

kinds.note: Sung while the lamp is waved before the deity.
Forty chaupais in praise of a deity, recited daily by millions.
Hymns of praise, most in Sanskrit, including ashtakams of eight verses.
Short sacred verses for daily prayer, study and japa.
Devotional songs of the saint-poets: Tulsidas, Surdas, Meera, Narsinh Mehta.

ganesh-chaturthi.note: Ten days of Ganeshotsav. In Maharashtra every aarti session opens with Sukhkarta Dukhharta.

navratri.note: Nine nights of the Goddess. Jai Ambe Gauri is sung every morning and evening.

dussehra.note: Ram’s victory over Ravan, the day after Navratri ends.

dhanteras.note: Lamps are lit at dusk and Lakshmi is worshipped for the coming year.

diwali.note: Lakshmi Puja at dusk. Most homes begin with the Ganesh aarti, then Lakshmi.

govardhan.note: Offerings to Krishna as Giridhar, who lifted Govardhan hill.

shravan.note: Shiv’s month; Mondays are kept with special devotion.

holi.note: The festival of colours, dear to Krishna’s Braj.

hanuman-jayanti.note: Hanuman’s birth, on Chaitra Purnima in North India.

satyanarayan.note: Om Jai Jagdish Hare is the aarti of the katha.

sundarkand.note: Recitation of the Sundarkand, usually closed with Hanuman’s aarti.

daily.note: Sung any day, morning or evening.

closing.note: Recited as the flame is offered at the end.

basant-panchami.note: Saraswati Puja at the start of spring. Students place their books before the goddess.

chhath.note: Offerings to the setting and rising Sun, kept with great devotion in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh.

gita-jayanti.note: The day Krishna taught the Gita to Arjun, on Margashirsha Shukla Ekadashi.

morning.note: Short prayers for the start of the day or before study.

meals.note: Recited before eating, offering the food first.

weekdays.note: Many offer water to the rising sun and recite the Gayatri mantra.
Many homes also worship Durga on Tuesdays.
Durga and Santoshi Mata are also worshipped on Fridays.
There’s no Shani aarti in the collection yet.

about: Navratri means “nine nights”. Sharad Navratri, the autumn one, begins on the first day of the bright half of Ashvin and is the greatest of the four Navratris in the year; Chaitra Navratri in spring ends on Ram Navami, and the two Gupta Navratris of Magh and Ashadh are kept quietly by those who know them.

For nine nights the Goddess is worshipped in nine forms, the Navdurga, one each night, from Shailputri, daughter of the mountain, to Siddhidatri, giver of perfection. The Durga Saptashati tells why: the gods, helpless before Mahishasur and later Shumbh and Nishumbh, poured their power into one Goddess, and she fought and won. The tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates her victory and Ram’s victory over Ravan, whom he fought after worshipping the Goddess.

customs.t: On the first morning a kalash of water, crowned with mango leaves and a coconut, is set up as the seat of the Goddess, often beside a bed of soil sown with barley (jau or jawara) that sprouts through the nine days. Many homes keep an akhand jyoti, a lamp that is not allowed to go out until Navami.
Morning and evening, families sing the Durga aarti and recite the Durga Chalisa, and those who can read the Durga Saptashati, either whole each day or divided across the nine days.
Many fast through the nine days or on the first and last, eating fruit, milk, and dishes of kuttu, singhara, sabudana and samak rice, without grain, onion or garlic. Others fast only on Ashtami.

On Ashtami or Navami, nine young girls, seen as forms of the Goddess, and often one boy as Langur (Bhairav), are invited home, their feet washed, and they are fed halwa, puri and black chana and given gifts.

Bengal celebrates Durga Puja from Shashthi to Dashami in pandals, with Sandhi Puja at the meeting of Ashtami and Navami. Gujarat dances garba and dandiya every night. Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra set out golu, steps of dolls. Kerala and the South keep Saraswati and Ayudha Puja on Navami, and children begin their learning on Vijayadashami. Mysuru and Kullu hold their famous Dasara processions.

days.about: Sati, born again as the daughter of Himavan, king of the mountains, after giving up her life at her father Daksh’s sacrifice. As Parvati she would once more become Shiv’s wife. She is worshipped on the first day, together with the kalash.
days.look: Rides the bull Nandi, holds a trident in her right hand and a lotus in her left, with a crescent moon on her brow.
days.offer: Pure ghee is commonly offered on the first day.

read.why: Names the nine Durgas; read before the Saptashati

days.about: Parvati as the young ascetic who undertook years of fierce tapas, living on leaves and then on nothing at all, to win Shiv as her husband. She stands for steadfastness and devotion that does not give up.
days.look: Walks barefoot in white, holding a japa mala in her right hand and a kamandalu, a water-pot, in her left.

days.means: She who wears a bell-shaped moon
days.about: Parvati as Shiv’s bride, a half-moon shaped like a bell on her forehead. The sound of her bell drives away demons and fear, and brings her devotees courage and peace.
days.look: Golden in colour, with ten arms bearing weapons, riding a lion, ready for battle yet calm.
days.offer: Milk, or kheer made with milk, is commonly offered.

read.why: The Shakradi Stuti, where the gods ask her bell to protect them

days.means: She whose warmth holds the cosmic egg
days.about: When there was only darkness, she created the universe with a gentle smile. She lives in the core of the sun and gives it its light and energy.
days.look: Eight-armed (Ashtabhuja), holding a kamandalu, bow, arrow, lotus, a pot of nectar, discus, mace and japa mala, riding a lion.

read.why: Ya Devi Sarvabhuteshu: the Goddess present in every being

days.about: The mother of Skanda, also called Kartikeya, the commander of the gods’ army. Worshipping her, it is said, brings the grace of her son too.
days.look: Seated on a lotus, which is why she is also called Padmasana, with the child Skanda on her lap; four-armed, holding lotuses, and riding a lion.

read.why: Sita’s prayer to the mother of Ganesh and six-faced Skanda

days.about: Born in the hermitage of the sage Katyayan, she is the warrior form who slew Mahishasur. The gopis of Braj worshipped her for a month to win Krishna as their beloved. In Bengal, Durga Puja begins on this day.
days.look: Four-armed, holding a sword and a lotus, the other hands raised in blessing and reassurance, riding a lion.

read.why: The gods praise Katyayani as Narayani
The best-known verse of the Narayani Stuti

days.about: The fiercest of the nine, the night that swallows all darkness. She destroyed Raktabeej and every evil force. Though terrifying to see, she always brings good to her devotees, so she is also called Shubhankari.
days.look: Dark as night, hair loose, a necklace flashing like lightning, three eyes and fire on her breath; four-armed with a sword and an iron hook, riding a donkey.

read.why: The chalisa, which sings of her terrible Kalika form
An aarti to the slayer of Mahishasur

days.about: After Parvati’s long austerities her body had grown dark with dust; Shiv washed her with the waters of the Ganga and she shone white as jasmine and the moon. Durga Ashtami, with kanya pujan and havan in many homes, falls on this day.
days.look: Dressed all in white, riding a white bull, four-armed, with a trident and a damru.

read.why: Said at kanya pujan and the havan

days.about: She grants every siddhi, every spiritual power and attainment. By her grace, it is said, half of Shiv’s body became the Goddess, and he became Ardhanarishvar. On Navami Navratri closes with kanya pujan, havan and, in the South, Ayudha and Saraswati Puja.
days.look: Seated on a lotus, four-armed with a discus, conch, mace and lotus, attended by siddhas, gandharvas and gods.
days.offer: Sesame seeds, or halwa, puri and chana for the girls of kanya pujan, are commonly offered.

read.why: The Narayani Stuti, to close the path

after.t: Vijayadashami: the Goddess’s victory over Mahishasur and Ram’s over Ravan. The kalash is moved, the sprouted barley is shared as a blessing, and in Bengal the images are taken for visarjan.
